output.title: What churn signals hide before the customer leaves
output.body:
Most churn does not arrive as a dramatic cancellation. It usually shows up first in quieter signals: fewer orders, longer gaps between purchases, repeated support questions, or a customer who stops using one part of the service while still paying out of habit. The job is not to chase every wobble. It is to separate active signals from passive erosion.

Active signals are the obvious ones: a cancellation notice, a payment problem, a sharp complaint. Those need a human decision now. Passive signals are slower and easier to miss. In an online shop, for example, a customer who used to buy every week and then goes three weeks with no order is not proof of churn, but it is a signal worth checking.

The bounded workflow decision is simple: decide which signals your team can already see in a spreadsheet, CRM, support inbox, or payment records, and which ones stay invisible until the customer is gone. If the data already exists, a small workflow can flag the pattern and route it to manual review. It should not decide the response on its own.

A practical next step is to pull the last 12 months of order history, support tickets, login activity, and payment records, then pick two or three customers who left or went quiet. Write down the first signal you could have seen at the time. That manual audit will tell you whether the workflow is worth building.
